title: We Taught Kids to Question Everything, Now What
author: Murray Sutcliffe
summary: Murray Sutcliffe, a Theory of Knowledge teacher, questions the critical-thinking mantra of "question everything" that he once taught enthusiastically. He frames the essay around a teenage memory of his family's faith in the Power Balance bracelet, noting that his first instinct was belief and doubt came later. He then argues that students today inherit the opposite condition: drawing on Karl Mannheim's theory of generations and Hannah Arendt's view of education, he suggests that young people raised with Google, YouTube and endless comment sections take pervasive doubt as their starting point. The key move is a rereading of Descartes: methodological skepticism was a route to firmer knowledge, not permission to distrust everything, and Descartes wanted his apples back in the basket. Using Onora O'Neill's distinction between trust and trustworthiness, Sutcliffe argues that more information does not produce better judgment and that critical-thinking instruction must teach students where to place trust, not only how to withdraw it. He closes with practical classroom moves: ask what evidence would change a student's mind, require provisional commitment, and practise with trustworthy sources rather than only dodgy ones.
points: Sutcliffe argues that "question everything" misreads Descartes, whose radical doubt was a method for rebuilding certainty rather than a case for permanent suspicion.

Using Mannheim, he claims today's students inherit doubt as the normal condition of the information environment rather than learning it through experience, which changes what critical-thinking teaching must do.
Skepticism can justify withdrawing trust but says nothing about where to place it, so questioning the scientist does not make the podcaster more reliable.
Following Onora O'Neill, he warns that dumping more evidence on people does not improve judgment unless they can assess what they are looking at.

His classroom fixes: ask what a student would need to see to believe a claim, make students commit to a currently best explanation (teaching fallibilism), and stop teaching source evaluation only with fake or conspiratorial material.
quotes: What Descartes was doing is what we call methodological skepticism: he was using doubt strategically to help him arrive at a certainty about the world. This practice has commonly been translated in modern speak to mean: “question everything”.
There is an important distinction here: Kids don’t simply experience new technologies or social changes differently. They inherit as normal what previous generations experienced as change.

And this is why my initial advice of “question everything” might have felt so compelling. It gives us permission to remain suspicious without ever deciding what deserves our belief; because it is easier to default to doubt than struggle for truth.

We need trust in expertise and institutions for society to continue functioning. Scepticism can give us good reasons to withdraw that trust, but on its own it tells us very little about where we should place it instead. Questioning the scientist doesn’t make the podcaster more reliable.

The natural response to this is to make more evidence more readily available so we can judge the science ourselves. But more information doesn’t mean better judgment. O’Neill explains that information only helps if people can assess what they’re looking at.

We have been taught that critical thinking is largely about the ability to interrogate claims. But perhaps the information environment now requires us to become equally good at teaching students to decide which claims deserve their trust. Ultimately, Descartes wanted his apples back in his basket, not scattered around the floor.

The word “currently” matters; it teaches them the theory of fallibilism. They’re practicing making the best judgment given their available evidence, even if that judgement turns out later to be wrong.
We often teach source evaluation by deliberately giving students dodgy sources (conspiracy theories, fake news etc.). But if that’s all we practice, we are essentially training suspicion.
